title: Periodic material cells of greatest bulk modulus (QV-Topo 1)
statement: A periodic cell of 40 x 40 square elements describes a two-dimensional material: every element is solid (Young's modulus 1, Poisson's ratio 0.3, plane stress) or void (Young's modulus 1e-9). The cell must have at most the cell's volume fraction of solid elements, a minimum feature size of 2 (every solid element in a 2 x 2 solid square and every void one in a 2 x 2 void square, wrapping around the cell), no point contacts, and its solid elements must form one connected piece that wraps around the cell in both directions (a connected material). QV-Topo 1 (checkers/topopt_check.py, standard library only) computes the homogenised stiffness tensor C (Voigt notation, engineering shear strain) by the energy method with periodic boundary conditions: for each unit average strain the periodic displacement that minimises the energy, solved by our own direct solver, the same digits on every machine. THIS IS A NUMERICAL MODEL of an idealised material. The score is the bulk modulus under a hydrostatic strain, (C11 + C22 + 2 C12) / 4, rounded down to 0.000001. The two-dimensional Hashin-Shtrikman upper bound bounds the exact bulk modulus of every cell, isotropic or not, and is shown with each cell; bilinear elements are slightly too stiff, so on the grid only discretisation error could pass it. The headline cell: volume fraction 0.5.
submission: Text file: 40 lines of 40 characters 0 or 1 (the top row first). See checkers/topopt_check.py.
score: the bulk modulus under a hydrostatic strain, (C11 + C22 + 2 C12) / 4, rounded down to 0.000001 (larger is better)
context: Designing the microstructure of a material for given elastic properties (inverse homogenisation, Sigmund 1994) is how architected materials and metamaterials are designed. For the bulk modulus there is a rigorous upper bound, the Hashin-Shtrikman bound, and microstructures that reach it are known in the limit of infinitely fine geometry; on a fixed grid with a minimum feature size the question is how close a single cell can come. Papers report designs on their own grids and filters, often with grey elements, so no published value applies under these settings: every cell is a first entry, shown with its distance to the bound. Each cell also keeps a baseline: a plain square grid of bars.
references: O. Sigmund, Materials with prescribed constitutive parameters: an inverse homogenization problem, Int. J. Solids Struct. 31 (1994) 2313-2329
O. Sigmund, A new class of extremal composites, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 48 (2000) 397-428
E. Andreassen, C. S. Andreasen, How to determine composite material properties using numerical homogenization, Comput. Mater. Sci. 83 (2014) 488-495: the energy method used here
L. Xia, P. Breitkopf, Design of materials using topology optimization and energy-based homogenization approach in Matlab, Struct. Multidisc. Optim. 52 (2015) 1229-1241

Z. Hashin, S. Shtrikman, A variational approach to the theory of the elastic behaviour of multiphase materials, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 11 (1963) 127-140; Z. Hashin, On elastic behaviour of fibre reinforced materials of arbitrary transverse phase geometry, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 13 (1965) 119-134: the two-dimensional bounds
G. W. Milton, The Theory of Composites, Cambridge University Press (2002)

cells.statement: Find a connected 0/1 periodic cell of {n} x {n} elements, at most {volfrac} solid, minimum feature size {k}, with the largest hydrostatic bulk modulus in the QV-Topo 1 model.
cells.submission: Text file: {n} lines of {n} characters 0 or 1 (checkers/topopt_check.py cell bulk {n} {volfrac} {k} {floor} FILE).
cells.bound_source: the two-dimensional Hashin-Shtrikman upper bound f k1 m1 / ((1 - f) k1 + m1) for a porous material (k1 = 1/1.4, m1 = 1/2.6: the plane-stress bulk and shear moduli of the solid); it bounds the exact hydrostatic bulk modulus of every cell, isotropic or not (the model's value on the grid can pass it only by discretisation error)
